entries.reason: a departure from 12.0 in how a batch request is carried out: iOS 6 has no SQL for it, so a batch delete finds the objects with its fetch request in a private context of its own and deletes and saves them, and a batch update finds them with its predicate and sets the values of the properties on them and saves; that applies delete rules, validation and the model's rules to the values, and posts a did save notification of that context, none of which iOS 12 does, and the objects of the calling context are already up to date afterwards where iOS 12 leaves them as they were until they are merged. A fetch request given to it is executed as -executeFetchRequest:error: and answers the array, and any other request is executed by the release's own coordinator and answers what that answers
entries.effect: an asynchronous fetch request answers its result at once and delivers the fetch to the request's block on the context's queue; a batch update request sets the values of what its predicate finds in the store; a batch delete request removes what its fetch request finds; both answer a result of the request's result type, nil and the error when the fetch or the save fails; a fetch request answers the array of its results; any other request goes to the release's own coordinator
entries.source: CoreData of the arm64 shared cache of iOS 12.0: -[NSManagedObjectContext executeRequest:error:] at 0x1839f0f58 reads the request type and hands a batch request to the coordinator, and -[NSManagedObjectContext _executeAsynchronousFetchRequest:] for the asynchronous fetch; the host's Core Data, run beside the port on a twin store, for what each request removes, sets, delivers and answers; an iPad 2 running 6.1.3
